title: Modules: ES Modules and CommonJS
summary: Split code into files with import and export, understand when a .js file is an ES module or a CommonJS module, mix the two systems, and find your file's folder with import.meta.
introduction: Real programs are many files, and a module system decides how those files share code. Node has two: the modern standard ES modules (`import`/`export`) and its original CommonJS system (`require`/`module.exports`). You will write ES modules, but you will still meet CommonJS in older packages, tutorials and configuration files, so this lesson teaches both, explains how Node decides which one a file uses, and shows the small differences that trip people up, such as the missing `__dirname`.
learningObjectives: Export and import values with named and default exports
Explain how the .mjs, .cjs extensions and the type field choose a module system
Use CommonJS modules from ES modules and locate files with import.meta.dirname

blocks.text: A module is a file with its own private scope. Nothing inside it is visible to other files unless the module explicitly **exports** it, and a file can only use what it explicitly **imports**. That rule keeps names from colliding, makes dependencies between files visible at the top of each file, and lets Node load only what a program needs.
With `"type": "module"` in `package.json` (set up in the previous lesson), every `.js` file is an ES module. A module can have any number of **named exports** and at most one **default export**:

blocks.title: math.js
main.js

items: Named exports are imported inside braces and must use the exported name (or be renamed with `as`: `{ add as sum }`).
The default export is imported without braces under any name you like; `describe` could have been called `info`.
Relative paths **must** start with `./` or `../` and **must** include the file extension. Node does not guess `.js` the way bundlers do.
Built-in modules use the `node:` prefix (`import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises'`); packages from npm use their bare name (`import express from 'express'`).

blocks.title: The missing extension
blocks.text: Writing `import { add } from './math'` fails with `Error [ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND]: Cannot find module '/home/ada/bookshelf/math' imported from /home/ada/bookshelf/main.js` followed by the hint `Did you mean to import "./math.js"?`. The same applies to folders: `import x from './utils'` does not load `./utils/index.js` in an ES module. Always write the full file name.
Node decides per file, using the extension first and the nearest `package.json` second:

rows: CommonJS by default. Node 22.7 and later detect `import`/`export` syntax and re-parse the file as an ES module, printing a warning that asks you to add the `type` field

blocks.text: CommonJS is what Node used before the ES module standard existed, and millions of packages still ship it. A CommonJS file assigns to `module.exports` and loads other files with the `require()` function, which runs synchronously and returns whatever the other file exported:

blocks.title: use-logger.cjs
blocks.code:
const { log } = require('./logger.cjs');

log('CommonJS still works');

blocks.text: CommonJS files also get two free variables, `__dirname` and `__filename`, holding the folder and path of the current file. ES modules do not have them, and they do not have `require` either; using any of the three in an ES module throws a `ReferenceError`.
An ES module can import a CommonJS file directly: the whole `module.exports` object arrives as the default import, so you rarely need to touch old code to use it.

blocks.title: app.js
blocks.code:
import logger from './logger.cjs';

logger.log('called from an ES module');

blocks.text: The other direction also works in current Node: since version 22.12, `require()` can load an ES module as long as that module contains no top-level `await`. And if you ever need a real `require` inside an ES module (for example to load a `.cjs` config), `createRequire(import.meta.url)` from `node:module` builds one.
Finding your own folder with import.meta

Because `__dirname` is missing, ES modules use `import.meta` instead. `import.meta.url` is the `file://` URL of the current module, and Node 20.11 and later add `import.meta.dirname` and `import.meta.filename` as plain paths. Combine them with `node:path` to build paths that work no matter which folder the program was started from:

blocks.title: paths.js
node paths.js (on Windows the last two lines use backslashes and a drive letter)

blocks.text: Importing JSON and loading modules on demand
JSON files can be imported directly when you add an *import attribute* that declares the type, which prevents a server from smuggling executable code into what you expected to be data:

blocks.title: settings.js (config.json contains { "name": "bookshelf", "port": 3000 })
blocks.code:
import config from './config.json' with { type: 'json' };

console.log(`${config.name} will listen on port ${config.port}`);

blocks.text: Finally, `import()` as a function returns a promise and loads a module only when that line runs. It is useful for optional features or heavy dependencies: `const { DatabaseSync } = await import('node:sqlite');` loads SQLite support only if the program actually needs it.

blocks.title: One system per project
blocks.text: Pick ES modules for new projects and keep the whole project consistent. Use `.cjs` only for files that must be CommonJS, such as a configuration file a tool insists on loading with `require`.

questions.question: A project has `"type": "module"` in package.json. Which file is treated as CommonJS?
questions.explanation: The .cjs extension always means CommonJS, regardless of the type field. .js files follow the type field and .mjs files are always ES modules.

questions.question: Inside an ES module, the folder of the current file is available as `import.meta.___`.
questions.explanation: import.meta.dirname (Node 20.11+) replaces the CommonJS __dirname variable; import.meta.filename replaces __filename.
